title: The Professor Who Kept Buying Chocolate
author: Robert Cialdini
wiifm: Yesterday you met the fast, automatic part of the mind. Today you meet the people who learned to press its buttons for money. Robert Cialdini was a social psychologist who kept being talked into things, so he went undercover among salespeople, fundraisers and recruiters to find out how they did it. What he found became six principles that now sit behind almost every landing page, sales script and advert you will ever write. Joe, you will learn how to use them honestly, and how to spot when they are being used on you, or on a vulnerable client.

b: Robert Cialdini was born in April 1945 and grew up in Wisconsin. He liked to describe his background as a puzzle of belonging: an Italian family, living in a largely Polish neighbourhood, in the old German city of Milwaukee, in an otherwise rural state. He learned early that people decide who they are partly by noticing who they are with. That idea would come back, decades later, as the last chapter of his life's work.

He studied psychology, took his doctorate at the University of North Carolina in 1970, did further research at Columbia, and in 1971 joined Arizona State University, where he spent the rest of his career. By training he was an experimental social psychologist, running careful studies on students in laboratories.

By temperament, he admitted, he was a pushover. He opens Influence with a confession. For as long as he could remember he had been an easy mark for pedlars, fundraisers and operators of one sort or another. He would find himself the owner of unwanted magazine subscriptions and tickets to the sanitation workers' ball. That embarrassment, he said, was the real origin of the book. Why did a man who studied persuasion for a living say yes to things he did not want?
ch.cap: Cialdini at his door, arms full of unwanted magazines

ch.h: The Boy Scout and the chocolate bars
b: One evening a boy of eleven or twelve stopped him in the street. He was selling tickets to a Boy Scout circus, five dollars each. Cialdini declined. Then the boy said that if he did not want tickets, perhaps he would buy some of the big chocolate bars instead, only a dollar each. Cialdini bought two. He does not even like chocolate.

Walking away with the bars, he realised that something precise had happened. The boy had made a large request, accepted the refusal, and retreated to a smaller one. That retreat felt like a concession, and Cialdini had felt obliged to make a concession in return. Back at the university he and his students tested it. In a 1975 study they asked students on campus to chaperone a group of juvenile offenders on a trip to the zoo. Only about one in six agreed. But when they first asked for something huge, two hours a week as a counsellor for two years, and then retreated to the zoo trip after the inevitable refusal, about half agreed.

This became known as the rejection-then-retreat technique, or the door in the face. It is one form of the first and strongest principle in the book: reciprocation. We feel we must repay what others give us, whether a gift, a favour or a concession.

Notice what the boy did not do. He did not argue, flatter or pressure. He simply arranged the order of two requests. That is what unsettled Cialdini most. The technique worked on a trained psychologist who was paying attention, because it did not run through his reasoning at all.
ch.cap: A Boy Scout sells Cialdini two chocolate bars

b: Before the principles, Cialdini sets out the mechanism, and he begins with a mother turkey. Turkey hens are attentive mothers, but their care is triggered largely by one thing: the cheep-cheep sound of chicks. In research described by the animal behaviourist M. W. Fox, a hen would attack a stuffed polecat, its natural enemy, but would gather the same stuffed polecat under her wing if it contained a recorder playing chick sounds. Click, and the tape plays.

Humans have the same shortcuts, he argued, and mostly they serve us well. The world is too complicated to analyse everything. So we use reliable cues: expensive usually means good, experts usually know best, if everyone is doing it there is probably a reason. Click, whirr, and we act.

His favourite example came from a friend who ran a jewellery shop in Arizona. She could not shift a batch of turquoise, so before leaving on a trip she scribbled a note telling her head saleswoman to sell everything in the case at half price. The saleswoman misread it as double. The jewellery sold out. Tourists who knew little about turquoise were using price as a signal of quality.

In 1978 the Harvard psychologist Ellen Langer showed how thin the trigger can be. People queuing for a photocopier were asked to let someone go first. A request with a real reason worked well. But so did a request with an empty one, may I use the machine, because I have to make some copies. The word because was enough. Influence, Cialdini concluded, is the craft of triggering these shortcuts on purpose.
ch.cap: A turkey hen mothers a stuffed polecat playing chick sounds

b: Laboratory studies told him the shortcuts existed. He wanted to know how professionals used them in the wild. So, for about three years, he became what sociologists call a participant observer. He answered newspaper advertisements for sales trainees and learned to sell encyclopaedias, vacuum cleaners, portrait photography and dance lessons door to door. He hung around car showrooms, sat with fundraisers and telemarketers, and talked his way into advertising and public relations firms.

He found an enormous variety of tactics but a small number of underlying principles. Compliance professionals did not need to understand the psychology. Over generations, the techniques that worked survived and the ones that did not were dropped, much as in natural selection. He boiled them down to six: reciprocation, commitment and consistency, social proof, liking, authority and scarcity.

Reciprocation he had already met in the Boy Scout. In the field it was everywhere. The Hare Krishna movement in the 1970s had raised money at airports by first pressing a flower or a book into a traveller's hand as a gift, then asking for a donation. People resented it and still paid, often throwing the flower in a bin moments later. In a 1971 study by Dennis Regan at Cornell, a confederate who had bought a participant an unasked-for bottle of Coca-Cola sold about twice as many raffle tickets to that person afterwards, whether or not they liked him.
The honest version is simple. Give first, give something genuinely useful, and make it personal and unexpected. The dishonest version is a manufactured gift designed to create a debt.
ch.cap: Undercover, Cialdini sells encyclopaedias door to door

b: The second principle is commitment and consistency. Once we have taken a stand, we feel pressure, from inside and out, to behave in line with it. In a 1966 study by Jonathan Freedman and Scott Fraser in California, researchers posing as volunteers asked homeowners to put up a huge, ugly billboard on their front lawns saying Drive Carefully. Most refused. But in one group, people who had two weeks earlier agreed to display a small, three-inch sign saying Be a Safe Driver, about three quarters said yes. The small step had changed how they saw themselves.

Cialdini found the darkest version of this in accounts of Chinese prison camps for American soldiers during the Korean War. Rather than brutality, interrogators relied on tiny commitments: write a mild statement that America is not perfect, then expand on it, then read it aloud. Prisoners came to align their beliefs with what they had written in their own hand.

Commitments stick best when they are active, public, effortful and freely chosen. Written beats spoken. Car dealers used a version called the lowball: agree an attractive price, let the buyer fill in forms and imagine the car at home, then discover the price was an error. Many still bought, because they had built new reasons to want the car. The defence Cialdini offers is to listen to the pit of your stomach and ask: knowing what I know now, would I make the same choice again?

There is a quieter, kinder use of the same principle. In later research on missed appointments, getting patients to write the date and time on the card themselves, rather than having a receptionist write it, reduced no-shows. A small, freely chosen, written commitment did what reminders alone had not. Asking a client to confirm a callback time in their own words works for the same reason.
ch.cap: A giant Drive Carefully sign goes up on the lawn

b: The third principle is social proof. When we are unsure what to do, we look at what people like us are doing. Canned laughter works on television even though everyone knows it is fake. Bartenders salt their tip jars with a few notes. Advertisers call products the fastest-growing or the best-selling.

Cialdini's most chilling example was the murder of Kitty Genovese in New York in March 1964, reported at the time as a crime watched by thirty-eight neighbours who did nothing. The psychologists John Darley and Bibb Latané went on to show in experiments that people in a group are slower to help than people alone, partly because each person looks at the others, sees no alarm and concludes there is no emergency. That bystander effect has held up well. But the Genovese story itself was exaggerated. Later investigations, including an acknowledgement by The New York Times in 2016, found that far fewer people saw the attack and that some did call for help.

He analysed a darker case of the same mechanism: the mass suicide at Jonestown in Guyana in November 1978, where more than nine hundred followers of Jim Jones died. Cialdini argued that moving the group from San Francisco to an unfamiliar jungle had left them deeply uncertain, and that uncertain people take their cues from those around them. Once the first members complied, the rest followed. It is his interpretation rather than settled history, but it shows the principle at its most extreme.

His practical advice for an emergency is precise. If you need help in a crowd, single out one person, look at them and say: you, in the blue jacket, call an ambulance. Remove the uncertainty and you remove the paralysis.

Social proof works most strongly under uncertainty and among similar people. That is why reviews from customers in situations like the reader's own beat generic praise, and why a number of real clients helped is more persuasive than any adjective.
ch.cap: In a frozen crowd she points: you, call an ambulance

ch.h: Tupperware, white coats and the last cookie
b: The fourth principle is liking. We say yes to people we like, and we like people who are similar to us, who compliment us, who cooperate with us and who are familiar. Tupperware parties were his model case: the hostess's friends bought not from a company but from her. He also described Joe Girard, listed in the Guinness Book of Records as the world's greatest car salesman, who sent every customer a card each month carrying the same simple message, I like you.

The fifth is authority. We defer to experts and to the symbols of expertise: titles, uniforms, confident manner. Cialdini leaned on Stanley Milgram's obedience experiments at Yale in the early 1960s, in which ordinary people continued giving what they believed were dangerous electric shocks to a stranger because a man in a grey lab coat told them to. Later historians, notably Gina Perry, have shown that Milgram's procedures were less consistent than he reported and that many participants doubted the shocks were real, but the core finding, that authority powerfully overrides conscience, has been reproduced in milder forms.

The sixth is scarcity. Things are more attractive when they are rare or disappearing. In a 1975 study by Stephen Worchel, people rated identical chocolate chip cookies as more desirable when there were two in the jar rather than ten, and more desirable still when the jar had just gone from ten to two. Limited numbers, deadlines and the threat of losing a freedom all trigger the same reaction. It connects directly to Kahneman's loss aversion: the fear of missing out is a fear of loss.

Each principle has a defence, and the defence is never to abandon the shortcut altogether, because most of the time it serves you well. It is to notice when the cue has been faked. Is this gift a gift, or a bait? Is the crowd real? Is the expert actually expert in this, or just wearing the coat? Is the deadline real, and would I want this as much if there were plenty? A single honest question usually breaks the spell.
ch.cap: A lab coat urges the shock; two cookies wait

ch.h: Weapons, and the duty that comes with them
b: Influence came out in 1984 and sold slowly at first, partly because it had been written for ordinary readers rather than academics. It then became one of the most widely read business books ever published, with several million copies sold. Marketers adopted it as a manual. Cialdini was uneasy about that. He had written it, in large part, as a book of self-defence.

He also noticed that the principles get stronger as modern life gets busier. When we are rushed, tired, distracted or overloaded with information, we fall back on shortcuts more often, not less. That is exactly the state in which many people meet an advert or a sales call. It places a special duty on anyone persuading people who are stressed, frightened or short of money.

His central moral distinction is between using the principles to point to something real and using them to fake it. If a product genuinely is popular, saying so is honest social proof. Inventing reviews is theft. If stock genuinely is limited, saying so is fair. A countdown timer that resets every time the page reloads is a lie. The shortcuts exist because they are usually reliable, and every counterfeit makes them less reliable for everyone.

In later work, notably Pre-Suasion in 2016 and an expanded edition of Influence in 2021, he added a seventh principle, unity: we say yes to people we see as part of our own group, our family, our place, our tribe. It brought him back to the Italian boy in a Polish neighbourhood. Some of the studies he cited have since faced scrutiny in the replication debates that shook social psychology, but a large multi-laboratory replication published in 2021 supported one of his signature findings, the door in the face. For anyone working with people in debt or under pressure, the book is best read both ways: as a guide to honest persuasion, and as a list of the alarms to watch for when someone else is applying the pressure.
ch.cap: Influence held up as a shield against faked cues

take: Reciprocation is the strongest lever. Offer something genuinely useful, such as a free guide or a clear answer, before you ask for anything.
A refused large request makes a smaller follow-up feel like a concession. Present your premium option first, honestly, then the standard one.
Commitments that are active, written and freely chosen grow. Ask a lead for one small, easy step before the big one.
Social proof works best under uncertainty and among similar people. Use real testimonials from clients in situations close to the reader's own.
In a crowd nobody acts. When you need help, name one person and give them one clear task.
People defer to credible experts. Display genuine credentials like regulatory status prominently, and never borrow authority you do not have.
Limited time and stock are powerful because they trigger fear of loss. Use them only when true, or you burn trust and risk misleading customers.
When you feel pushed, ask whether, knowing what you know now, you would make the same choice again. If not, step back.
recall: What are Cialdini's six original principles?
Reciprocation, commitment and consistency, social proof, liking, authority and scarcity. He later added a seventh, unity, the pull of shared identity.
What did the Boy Scout teach Cialdini?

By asking for a five-dollar ticket and retreating to one-dollar chocolate bars, the boy made a concession that Cialdini felt obliged to repay. His 1975 zoo-trip study confirmed that this rejection-then-retreat technique sharply raises compliance.

It describes automatic responses triggered by a single cue, like the turkey hen mothering anything that plays chick sounds. Humans have similar shortcuts, such as treating high price as a sign of quality, which persuaders can trigger deliberately.
How did small commitments change behaviour in the lawn-sign study?

Homeowners who first agreed to display a small safe-driving sign were far more likely to accept a huge ugly billboard later. The small step changed how they saw themselves, so the bigger request felt consistent.
What is wrong with the usual Kitty Genovese story?

The claim that thirty-eight neighbours watched and did nothing was exaggerated, as later reporting and The New York Times acknowledged. The bystander effect itself is supported by experiments, but the famous case was not a clean example of it.
note: The Boy Scout, turquoise and undercover research stories come from Cialdini's own account in Influence. The cited studies, Regan 1971, Freedman and Fraser 1966, Cialdini and colleagues 1975, Langer 1978 and Worchel 1975, are real and documented, though some have small samples. The Genovese narrative was later shown to be exaggerated, and Milgram's methods have been criticised by Gina Perry and others.
words: The deep social rule that we feel obliged to repay what others give us.
The Boy Scout's retreat from tickets to chocolate felt like a gift, so Cialdini felt obliged to give something back and bought two bars.
In an experiment, an accomplice of the researcher who pretends to be an ordinary participant.
In Dennis Regan's 1971 study a confederate who bought people an unasked-for Coca-Cola sold them about twice as many raffle tickets.
The act of agreeing to a request, often without full conscious reasoning.
Cialdini went undercover among compliance professionals, the salespeople and fundraisers whose job is getting people to say yes.
A sales tactic of agreeing an attractive price and then withdrawing it once the buyer has committed.
Car dealers would discover an error in the price after the buyer had filled in forms, and many still bought.
The tendency of each person in a group to feel less duty to act because others could.
Darley and Latané showed that bystanders in a group are slower to help, which is why Cialdini advises naming one person in an emergency.
stories: The chocolate bars he did not want

One evening a boy of about eleven stopped Robert Cialdini, a professor of persuasion, and asked him to buy five-dollar tickets to a Boy Scout circus. Cialdini said no. Fine, said the boy, then how about some chocolate bars at only a dollar each? Cialdini bought two. He does not even like chocolate. Walking away, he realised what had happened. The boy had retreated from a big request to a small one, and the retreat felt like a concession that demanded one back. Cialdini went straight back to his lab and proved it worked on students too.

A friend of Cialdini's ran a jewellery shop in Arizona and could not shift a batch of turquoise. Before leaving on a trip she scribbled a note to her head saleswoman: everything in that case, times one half. The saleswoman misread it as times two. When the owner came back, the turquoise had sold out at double the price. Tourists who knew nothing about turquoise were using price as a shortcut for quality. Expensive usually means good, so click, whirr, they bought. It is Cialdini's favourite example of how our mental shortcuts can be triggered almost by accident.
The thirty-eight witnesses who were not

In March 1964 Kitty Genovese was murdered in New York, and the story told for decades was that thirty-eight neighbours watched and nobody helped. Psychologists John Darley and Bibb Latané went on to show in experiments that people in a crowd really are slower to help, because each looks at the others and sees no alarm. Cialdini made it a centrepiece of Influence. The twist is that the original story was exaggerated. Later investigations, acknowledged by The New York Times in 2016, found far fewer people saw the attack and some did call for help. The effect is real. The famous example was not.
biz: Reciprocity and social proof are powerful precisely because people searching for a secured loan are uncertain. Use them honestly on HomeownersLoan and Apply4Loan. Give first: answer the lead's actual question on WhatsApp in plain English, including that their home is at risk if they do not keep up repayments, before asking for documents. Show genuine reviews from homeowners in similar situations, never invented ones, and never a countdown timer or false limited offer. This week, audit every advert and landing page for any scarcity or popularity claim you cannot evidence, and track enquiry-to-application rate before and after.
A written commitment that protects the client

Cialdini notes that patients who wrote their own appointment details missed fewer appointments. Debt Support Direct loses help to missed callbacks, often from people overwhelmed by letters. After a first call, send a WhatsApp asking the client to reply confirming the callback time in their own words. It is a small, freely chosen commitment to a conversation, not to any debt solution, and the client can cancel freely. Measure callback attendance for four weeks against the previous month. Train advisers to spot when a client has been pushed elsewhere by fake urgency, and slow things down.
connects: Ogilvy argued that facts and genuine testimonials sell better than hype, the honest version of Cialdini's social proof and authority.
Haidt's account of tribal moral intuitions explains why Cialdini's seventh principle, unity, works so strongly on people who share a group.
Epictetus taught people to test each impression before assenting to it, an ancient version of Cialdini's pause to ask whether a cue has been faked.
recap:
Robert Cialdini grew up in Milwaukee in the nineteen fifties, an Italian boy in a Polish neighbourhood, and became a professor of social psychology in Arizona. He also had an embarrassing secret. He was a pushover. He kept buying magazine subscriptions and tickets he did not want, and he wanted to know why.

The answer arrived on a pavement. A Boy Scout asked him to buy circus tickets. He said no. The boy asked whether he would buy a couple of chocolate bars instead. He bought two, and he does not like chocolate. Back in his lab he proved what had happened. A refused big request makes a smaller one feel like a concession, and concessions demand repayment. That is reciprocation, the first and strongest principle. We repay gifts, favours and even retreats.

The second idea is the mechanism. Cialdini described a mother turkey that will cuddle a stuffed predator if it plays the sound of chicks. Humans have shortcuts too. A jeweller's turquoise sold out only when it was mistakenly priced at double, because tourists read price as quality. Most of the time these shortcuts serve us well. Influence is the craft of triggering them on purpose.

To see how professionals did it, he spent about three years undercover, training to sell encyclopaedias, vacuum cleaners and dance lessons. He found countless tactics but only six principles: reciprocation, commitment and consistency, social proof, liking, authority and scarcity. Small written commitments grow into big ones, like homeowners who agreed to a tiny road safety sign and then accepted a huge ugly billboard. Uncertain people copy those around them. We say yes to people we like and to people in white coats. And things become more desirable when they are disappearing.

The third idea is his warning. Busy, tired, stressed people lean on shortcuts more, not less, and that places a special duty on anyone persuading them. Using a principle to point at something true is honest. Real popularity, real limits, real expertise. Faking it, with invented reviews or a countdown that resets, is theft, and it makes the shortcuts less reliable for everyone.

The fourth idea is self defence. When you feel pushed, ask the stomach question: knowing what I know now, would I make the same choice again?

Influence came out in nineteen eighty four and sold millions. Marketers treated it as a manual. Cialdini meant it mostly as armour, and later added a seventh principle, unity, the pull of people we see as our own.

The line to remember: the strongest persuasion points to something true.
